newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU leaders meet to prepare for larger future.
newsitem.headline: EU leaders meet to prepare for larger future.

text.p: European Union leaders arrived in Dublin on Saturday for a special summit to re-invigorate efforts to prepare the bloc to incorporate up to 12 poorer states from central Europe and the Mediterranean.

With fears growing that talks on new treaty reforms ahead of enlargement are stagnating, the leaders are expected to call for negotiations to move along rapidly and be concluded as planned in the middle of next year.
"I think it's very important that we prepare Europe for the next century," said Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring, whose government currently holds the EU presidency.

"What we need today is to get re-affirmation from the leadership that we want to make progress...otherwise we're going to delay the whole process of enlargement and that has enormous implications for the rest of Europe," he added.

The leaders are also expected to discuss a wide range of foreign policy issues over dinner on Saturday night, including their frustration over being excluded from the latest Middle East peace moves by the United States.
Italy and France said on Friday they hoped the summit would make clear that the EU wanted to play a role in the process.
The one-day meeting in Dublin Castle was due to begin with a working lunch (1230 GMT) and end after dinner.

Ahead of the full talks, the leaders of the three Benelux countries -- founder members of the EU and ardent believers in the cause of deeper integration -- met to coordinate their positions. Leaders of Europe's socialist parties, including several summit participants, held separate talks.

At the centre of their concerns is the link between the six-month-old treaty talks -- formally an inter-governmental conference (IGC) -- and the goal of bringing in countries from tiny Malta to Poland.
To date the talks have homed in on what needs to be done, such as changing EU decision-making procedures and streamlining its institutions, but they have not led to any firm agreements.

Ireland, which is chairing the IGC, believes this is normal at this stage in a 15-month negotiation. It also says the IGC is on track to present a draft treaty to the regular EU summit in Dublin in December.

But the timing is acutely sensitive. Most leaders are anxious for the IGC to finish at the Amsterdam summit next June, a commitment reaffirmed on Saturday by Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok, whose government takes over the EU presidency in January.
Would-be members of the Union have been told enlargement negotiations will begin six months after the IGC ends.

And all governments, mindful of their knife-edge struggle to ratify the last major EU reforms in the Maastricht Treaty, are anxious to end the process well before the politically-charged decision in early 1998 on who can join the EU single currency.
Some worry, however, that IGC negotiators risk setting their sights too low.

"The inter-governmental conference must not be reduced to a routine car maintenance check where necessary reforms are being postponed until the future," Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson said this week.

But with British Prime Minister John Major under pressure from his increasingly Euro-sceptic Conservative party not to surrender any more sovereignty to the EU, progress before a general election which not come until May could be limited.

Although reaffirming on Saturday that he would not rule out membership of a single currency at this stage, as some right-wingers are demanding, Major is expected to take a firm line at the summit ahead of his party conference next week.

Officials said he was likely to be particularly critical of attempts by some socialist governments to insert an employment chapter into the treaty, arguing that flexible labour markets, not big EU spending, hold the key to jobs.
